title: General Topology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 400L General Topology curriculum, building on the 300L Metric Space Topology (MTH301) foundation: abstract topological spaces, bases and subspace/product topologies, continuity and homeomorphism, separation axioms, compactness and connectedness in general spaces (beyond the metric setting), quotient topology, and countability. Content is kept distinct from MTH301 by focusing on general topological spaces rather than metric-specific results.

questions.question: A topology on a set X is a collection tau of subsets of X satisfying:
options: X and the empty set belong to tau, arbitrary unions of members of tau are in tau, and finite intersections of members of tau are in tau
Only that X belongs to tau
Only finite unions of members are allowed
Every subset of X must belong to tau
questions.correct_answer: X and the empty set belong to tau, arbitrary unions of members of tau are in tau, and finite intersections of members of tau are in tau
questions.explanation: These three axioms define a topological space, generalizing the notion of open sets beyond metric spaces.

questions.question: In a topological space (X, tau), the members of tau are called:
questions.correct_answer: Open sets
questions.explanation: By definition, the topology tau is exactly the collection of open subsets of X.

questions.question: A set is closed in a topological space if:
options: It is a subset of a compact set
It contains only its boundary points
questions.correct_answer: Its complement is open
questions.explanation: Closed sets are defined as complements of open sets, mirroring the metric space definition but stated purely in terms of the topology.

questions.question: Unlike a metric space, a general topological space:
options: Need not have a distance function; its structure is defined directly by specifying which sets are open
Must always have a well-defined metric
questions.correct_answer: Need not have a distance function; its structure is defined directly by specifying which sets are open
questions.explanation: General topology abstracts away from distance, working purely with the axioms governing open sets, so not every topology arises from a metric.

questions.question: The discrete topology on a set X consists of:
options: Only X and the empty set
questions.correct_answer: All subsets of X
questions.explanation: In the discrete topology, every subset is declared open, making it the finest possible topology on X.

questions.question: The indiscrete (trivial) topology on a set X consists of:
options: Only X and the empty set
questions.correct_answer: Only X and the empty set
questions.explanation: The indiscrete topology is the coarsest possible topology, containing only the two required open sets.

questions.question: A collection B of subsets of X is a basis for a topology on X if every open set can be expressed as:
options: A union of members of B
An intersection of members of B
A complement of a member of B
questions.correct_answer: A union of members of B
questions.explanation: A basis generates the topology by taking arbitrary unions of its elements to produce every open set.

questions.question: Given a subset A of a topological space X, the subspace (relative) topology on A consists of sets of the form:
options: A intersected with U, for U open in X
Only open sets of X contained entirely in A
questions.correct_answer: A intersected with U, for U open in X
questions.explanation: The subspace topology is induced by intersecting every open set of X with A.

questions.question: The product topology on X times Y is generated by the basis of sets of the form:
options: U times V, where U is open in X and V is open in Y
Arbitrary subsets of X times Y
questions.correct_answer: U times V, where U is open in X and V is open in Y
questions.explanation: Products of open sets from each factor form a basis that generates the product topology.

questions.question: A function f: X to Y between topological spaces is continuous if:
options: The preimage f^(-1)(V) is open in X for every open set V in Y
The image f(U) is open in Y for every open U in X
questions.correct_answer: The preimage f^(-1)(V) is open in X for every open set V in Y
questions.explanation: This purely topological definition of continuity generalizes the epsilon-delta definition used in metric spaces.

questions.question: A homeomorphism between two topological spaces is:
options: A bijective continuous function whose inverse is also continuous
A function that preserves distances only
questions.correct_answer: A bijective continuous function whose inverse is also continuous
questions.explanation: A homeomorphism is the natural notion of isomorphism in topology, requiring continuity in both directions.

questions.question: Two homeomorphic topological spaces are considered, from the topological point of view, to be:
questions.correct_answer: Essentially the same (topologically equivalent)
questions.explanation: Homeomorphic spaces have identical topological properties, even if they look geometrically different.

questions.question: A topological space X is said to be T1 if:
options: For any two distinct points, each has a neighbourhood not containing the other; equivalently, singletons are closed
Any two points can be separated by disjoint open sets
questions.correct_answer: For any two distinct points, each has a neighbourhood not containing the other; equivalently, singletons are closed
questions.explanation: T1 is a weaker separation axiom than Hausdorff, characterized equivalently by every singleton set being closed.

questions.question: A topological space X is Hausdorff (T2) if:
options: Any two distinct points have disjoint open neighbourhoods
Every open cover has a finite subcover
questions.correct_answer: Any two distinct points have disjoint open neighbourhoods
questions.explanation: The Hausdorff property ensures points can be topologically separated, which guarantees uniqueness of limits of sequences and nets.

questions.question: Every metric space, with its metric topology, is automatically:
questions.correct_answer: Hausdorff
questions.explanation: For any two distinct points in a metric space, balls of radius less than half their distance apart are disjoint open neighbourhoods.

questions.question: A regular space (T3) requires that a point and a disjoint closed set can be separated by disjoint open sets, in addition to being:
questions.correct_answer: T1
questions.explanation: Regularity is usually defined as the separation-by-open-sets property combined with the T1 axiom to avoid degenerate cases.

questions.question: A normal space (T4) requires that two disjoint closed sets can be separated by disjoint open sets, in addition to being:
questions.correct_answer: T1
questions.explanation: Normality combines the closed-set separation property with T1, and every metric space is normal.

questions.question: In general topology, a collection of open sets {U_alpha} is called an open cover of X if:
questions.correct_answer: Their union equals X
questions.explanation: An open cover is any family of open sets whose union is the entire space.

questions.question: A topological space X is compact if:
options: Every open cover of X has a finite subcover
questions.correct_answer: Every open cover of X has a finite subcover
questions.explanation: This is the general topological definition of compactness, applicable even without any metric.

questions.question: The Heine-Borel characterization (closed and bounded equals compact) holds in R^n, but in general topological spaces, compactness:
options: Must be defined via open covers since 'bounded' has no meaning without a metric
Is always equivalent to closed and bounded
questions.correct_answer: Must be defined via open covers since 'bounded' has no meaning without a metric
questions.explanation: Boundedness is a metric concept, so general topology relies on the open cover definition of compactness instead.

questions.question: The continuous image of a compact space is:
questions.correct_answer: Always compact
questions.explanation: If f is continuous and X is compact, then f(X) is also compact, a key preservation theorem in topology.

questions.question: Tychonoff's theorem states that:
options: An arbitrary product of compact topological spaces is compact, in the product topology
Only finite products of compact spaces are compact
No product of compact spaces is compact
Products of compact spaces are never Hausdorff
questions.correct_answer: An arbitrary product of compact topological spaces is compact, in the product topology
questions.explanation: Tychonoff's theorem is one of the most important results in general topology and is equivalent to the Axiom of Choice.

questions.question: A topological space X is connected if:
options: It cannot be written as the union of two disjoint nonempty open sets
It has only one open set
questions.correct_answer: It cannot be written as the union of two disjoint nonempty open sets
questions.explanation: Connectedness is defined by the absence of a nontrivial partition of X into two disjoint open pieces.

questions.question: A subset that is both open and closed (clopen) in a connected space must be:
options: Either the whole space or the empty set
questions.correct_answer: Either the whole space or the empty set
questions.explanation: In a connected space, the only clopen sets are the trivial ones; any nontrivial clopen set would disconnect the space.

questions.question: The continuous image of a connected space is:
questions.correct_answer: Always connected
questions.explanation: Continuity preserves connectedness, just as it preserves compactness.

questions.question: A space X is path-connected if for every pair of points x, y in X:
options: There exists a continuous function gamma from [0,1] to X with gamma(0)=x and gamma(1)=y
There is an open set containing both x and y
questions.correct_answer: There exists a continuous function gamma from [0,1] to X with gamma(0)=x and gamma(1)=y
questions.explanation: Path-connectedness requires an explicit continuous path joining any two points, a stronger condition than mere connectedness.

questions.question: Every path-connected space is connected, but the converse:
options: Is not true in general; there exist connected spaces that are not path-connected
questions.correct_answer: Is not true in general; there exist connected spaces that are not path-connected
questions.explanation: The classic example is the topologist's sine curve, which is connected but not path-connected.

questions.question: The quotient topology on X/~ (X modulo an equivalence relation) is defined by declaring a set U in X/~ open if and only if:
options: Its preimage under the quotient map is open in X
The equivalence classes in U are singletons
questions.correct_answer: Its preimage under the quotient map is open in X
questions.explanation: This is the standard construction that makes the quotient map continuous and gives the finest topology doing so.

questions.question: A topological space is second countable if:
options: It has a countable basis for its topology
It has exactly two open sets
Every point has only finitely many neighbourhoods
questions.correct_answer: It has a countable basis for its topology
questions.explanation: Second countability is a countability axiom that many familiar spaces, such as R^n, satisfy.

questions.question: The closure of a set A in a topological space is defined as:
options: The smallest closed set containing A
The largest open set contained in A
The set of isolated points of A
questions.correct_answer: The smallest closed set containing A
questions.explanation: The closure is the intersection of all closed sets containing A, giving the smallest such closed set.

questions.question: The interior of a set A in a topological space is defined as:
options: The largest open set contained in A
The smallest closed set containing A
questions.correct_answer: The largest open set contained in A
questions.explanation: The interior is the union of all open sets contained in A, giving the largest such open set.

questions.question: A set A is dense in a topological space X if:
options: The closure of A equals X
questions.correct_answer: The closure of A equals X
questions.explanation: A dense set is one whose closure fills the whole space, meaning every nonempty open set meets A.
